screens.title: Interacting with the Fabric Gateway
screens.narratorSegment: The Fabric Gateway is the central simplification layer your client application uses to talk to a Hyperledger Fabric network. Instead of managing multiple direct connections to peers and ordering services, your app speaks to a Gateway peer using a single, well-defined A P I. This reduces complexity, lowers the chance of orchestration bugs, and makes it practical to maintain secure signing of transactions with identities stored in a wallet. In this lesson you will learn what the Gateway does, how to establish a connection from a Node. js client using a connection profile and a stored identity, and why discovery options and lifecycle management matter in both development and production. For example, enabling service discovery lets the Gateway learn which peers can endorse a transaction at runtime, so your application does not need hard-coded peer lists. A common development pitfall is using localhost certificates without the asLocalhost flag; we will show how that happens and how to avoid it. By the end, you'll be able to connect, sign, and gracefully disconnect from the Fabric network while handling common errors. How will you structure your app to reuse connections and report helpful errors to users?

screens.title: What the Gateway does
screens.narratorSegment: The Gateway is the SDK component that acts as a smart proxy between client applications and a Fabric network. Define it as a single, high-level interface that handles proposal distribution, endorsement collection, and interaction with the ordering service via a designated Gateway peer. Practically, think of the Gateway as a concierge at a large building: instead of calling every room directly, you give your request to the concierge who knows where to route it and collect approvals. For example, when your application wants to submit a transaction, the Gateway arranges which endorsing peers should sign the proposal according to chaincode endorsement policies and then packages the endorsed transaction for ordering. A common misconception is that the Gateway hides all network behavior; it does not erase visibility but simplifies it—service discovery still surfaces which peers are used, and you still need correct identities and connection profiles. The core takeaway is that the Gateway reduces the amount of topology and endorsement orchestration your app must perform, letting you focus on business logic. How might this change the structure of your client code when you move from a proof-of-concept to a production app?

content.html:
Core Concept Definition
Definition
A high-level SDK interface that abstracts multi-peer proposal routing, endorsement collection, and ordering interaction through a Gateway peer.
Analogy
Like a concierge who knows the building and coordinates approvals, the Gateway knows which peers to route proposals to and which orderer to use.
What the Gateway does in practice
  • Uses service discovery to determine available endorsing peers.
  • Signs and forwards proposals using the selected wallet identity.
  • Packages endorsed transactions for ordering.
Common misconception
The Gateway simplifies orchestration but doesn't remove the need for correct identities, certificates, and a valid connection profile.
Key takeaway
Use the Gateway to keep client code focused on business logic while relying on the SDK for network topology and endorsement mechanics.

screens.title: Gateway peer and service discovery
screens.narratorSegment: When a client connects to the Gateway, it establishes a connection to a specific peer or set of peers that act as a Gateway peer. That peer then performs service discovery on behalf of your application, returning information about endorsing peers, chaincode policies, and the ordering service. This dynamic discovery is what keeps your client resilient to topology changes: if a peer goes offline or a new peer joins, discovery updates let the Gateway route proposals to available endorsers without modifying the connection profile. For example, enabling discovery in the Node. js SDK instructs the Gateway to ask the connected peer which peers can satisfy the endorsement policy for a given chaincode. A common misunderstanding is believing discovery replaces the connection profile; it does not. The connection profile still provides initial endpoints and TLS certificate locations. Service discovery simply augments that runtime with up-to-date topology information. Practically, use discovery. enabled:true in production to avoid hard-coded peer lists, and ensure firewall rules allow peer-to-peer communication that discovery requires. What checks will you add to ensure discovery can reach peers in your environment?

keyIdea.title: Discovery enables resilience
keyIdea.text: Service discovery lets the Gateway find endorsers and ordering nodes at runtime so clients don't need fixed topology.

content.html:
Process Flow
Gateway peer and service discovery
How discovery keeps a client app aware of the network's current state.
Step-by-step
  1. Client opens gateway.connect with a connection profile and wallet identity.
  2. Gateway connects to the designated peer(s) listed in the profile.
  3. Gateway requests discovery data: endorsers, chaincode endorsement policy, and orderer info.
  4. Gateway caches runtime topology to route proposals and prepare transaction submission.
Why this matters
Discovery prevents brittle client configs and lets the network change without requiring client updates.
Common mistake
Assuming discovery will fix incorrect TLS paths or unreachable peers; discovery needs reachable endpoints and valid certificates to succeed.
Checkpoints
  • Confirm firewall rules between gateway peer and other peers.
  • Ensure connection profile lists at least one reachable peer for bootstrap.

screens.title: gateway.connect() options explained
screens.narratorSegment: The gateway. connect call requires a connection profile and an options object. Understanding each option is essential to make a reliable connection. The wallet option points the Gateway to a Wallets. newFileSystemWallet instance so the Gateway can retrieve the x509 credentials to sign proposals. The identity option is a string naming the stored identity; every transaction and query is signed by that identity. Discovery options are typically an object with enabled and asLocalhost flags. discovery. enabled:true turns on service discovery, which you want in production to learn topology dynamically. discovery. asLocalhost:true is a development convenience used when test networks generate TLS certs with localhost hostnames; it tells the SDK to override connection-hostnames with localhost during TLS verification. A frequent misconception is to leave asLocalhost:true in production. Doing so masks hostname mismatches and weakens certificate verification. A concrete example: gateway. connect(ccp, { wallet, identity: 'appUser', discovery: { enabled: true, asLocalhost: true } }) will work for a local test-network, but for a deployed cluster you should set asLocalhost to false and ensure your connection profile has real hostnames that match certificate SANs. What verification will you build into startup scripts to detect mismatched hostnames?

Definition
gateway.connect() options explained
Key options
wallet: a Wallet instance used to retrieve credentials for signing.
identity: the name of the identity to use from the wallet for all requests.
discovery: { enabled, asLocalhost } controls service discovery and dev TLS behavior.
Example
gateway.connect(ccp, { wallet, identity: 'appUser', discovery: { enabled: true, asLocalhost: true } }) — good for test-network development.

screens.title: Dissecting gateway.connect() in app.js
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the typical Node. js call that opens the Gateway connection and what each line accomplishes. First, you create a new Gateway instance and prepare your connection profile and wallet. Next, gateway. connect is called with the profile and options. The wallet contains the enrolled identity that will sign proposals, so the connect call retrieves the identity and prepares the client TLS and signing material. If discovery is enabled, the gateway asks the connected peer for the endorsement layout and orderer information. Important runtime checks include verifying that the wallet contains the named identity and that the connection profile file exists and points to correct TLS certificate paths. A concrete example from the chapter shows the single-line call with options: gateway. connect(ccp, { wallet, identity: 'appUser', discovery: { enabled: true, asLocalhost: true } });. A common mistake is not checking for a missing identity before connecting; always call await wallet. get('appUser') and handle null. Closing question: when you structure your startup code, where will you add validation so connection failures are caught early and reported with clear remediation steps?

screens.title: Robust error handling and disconnect logic
screens.narratorSegment: Robust applications wrap gateway connection logic in try/catch/finally so resources are always released and errors are informative. The chapter provides a full app. js pattern: declare gateway outside the try block so finally can access it, load and validate the connection profile, initialize the wallet, check the presence of the appUser identity, call gateway. connect, and then disconnect in the finally block. This pattern ensures that even if connect fails or an exception is thrown later, gateway. disconnect is attempted, preventing resource leaks. A concrete, hands-on example logs each step: loading the profile, initializing the wallet, finding the identity, attempting to connect, and disconnecting. A common misconception is that disconnect is only needed on normal shutdown; in fact, an uncaught failure that skips disconnect can leave file handles or sockets open. For long-running services, open the Gateway once at startup and reuse it rather than connect/disconnect per transaction. Reflect: where in your code will you centralize gateway lifecycle management so that retry logic and observability are simple to add? Robust error handling and disconnect logic means use try/catch/finally to guarantee gateway.disconnect runs and prevents resource leaks, while logging clear error messages.. In practical terms, using try/catch/finally to ensure graceful teardown. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Hands-on Activity
Robust error handling and disconnect logic
Why this pattern matters
Declaring the gateway variable outside try allows finally to call disconnect even if connect throws. Logging the error message and stack trace helps debugging and supports retry decisions.

Always attempt to disconnect in finally and centralize lifecycle management for long-running apps.

screens.title: asLocalhost: development vs production
screens.narratorSegment: The asLocalhost flag in discovery configuration instructs the SDK to override hostnames in the connection profile with localhost during TLS verification. This is useful when using the test-network because generated TLS certificates often have localhost hostnames. In development, setting asLocalhost to true prevents TLS handshake failures caused by hostname mismatches. However, in production this should be false since production networks use real DNS names or IPs that must match certificate SANs during verification. A concrete contrast: on a developer machine with test-network, asLocalhost:true prevents errors where the certificate lists peer0. org1. example. com but the endpoint is localhost. In production, forcing localhost would hide real hostname mismatches and could break certificate validation or security. People sometimes mistakenly keep asLocalhost:true across environments for convenience; this risks deploying with incorrect certificates or unreachable hosts. A quick verification step is to run a TLS handshake check or confirm the certificate SANs match the hostnames in your connection profile before toggling asLocalhost off. asLocalhost: development vs production means use aslocalhost only for local test networks; disable it in production where certificates and dns must match.. In practical terms, when to use aslocalhost and what it changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison
asLocalhost: development vs production
Development (test-network)
  • Certificates often reference localhost.
  • Set asLocalhost: true to override hostnames for TLS verification.
  • Prevents hostname mismatch errors in local runs.
Production
  • Use real DNS hostnames or IPs in the connection profile.
  • Set asLocalhost: false — do not override hostnames.
  • Certificates must match hostnames used for TLS verification.
Quick check
Run a certificate inspection or attempt a TLS handshake from the client machine to ensure the certificate SANs match the hostnames before turning off asLocalhost.

screens.title: Gateway lifecycle in long-running applications
screens.narratorSegment: Long-running applications should open a single Gateway connection at startup and reuse that gateway object for the application's lifetime. Opening and closing connections for every transaction is inefficient and will add latency and resource consumption. The recommended pattern is: on startup, validate the connection profile and wallet identity, call gateway. connect, store the gateway instance in a module or service layer, then use getNetwork and getContract for interactions. On graceful shutdown, call gateway. disconnect to free sockets and file handles. A concrete pattern is to wrap connect in a startup function and export a getGateway helper that returns the established gateway instance. A common mistake is failing to handle transient network interruptions: implement reconnection or retries with exponential backoff rather than repeatedly reestablishing connections in tight loops. Observability matters here — add health checks that verify the gateway is connected and can perform a simple query so orchestration systems can restart or repair as needed. Where will you put your gateway singleton so it is accessible but still safely cleaned up on shutdown? Gateway lifecycle in long-running applications means create one gateway at startup, reuse it for all interactions, and disconnect on shutdown to conserve resources and lower latency.. In practical terms, open once, reuse often — performance and resource considerations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow
Gateway lifecycle in long-running applications
Recommended lifecycle
  1. Startup: validate config and wallet, call gateway.connect once.
  2. Runtime: reuse gateway for getNetwork and getContract calls.
  3. Shutdown: call gateway.disconnect to free resources.
Expose a small gateway service that returns the active instance. Add a health-check endpoint that runs a simple query to verify connectivity for orchestration systems.
Performance note
Reusing a gateway reduces connection overhead and lowers transaction latency compared with connect per request.
Operational tip
Implement graceful shutdown hooks so gateway.disconnect always runs on process exit signals.

screens.title: Common connection errors and fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Connecting to a distributed Fabric network can produce a handful of repeatable errors. Connection refused usually means a network component is not running or the address in your connection profile is unreachable; verify the test-network is up and endpoints are reachable. TLS handshake errors often indicate incorrect tlsCACerts paths or hostname mismatches; check that the certificate file paths in the connection profile exist and that asLocalhost is set appropriately for development. Core Concept
Common connection errors and fixes
Error: Connection Refused
Cause: peer or orderer not running or unreachable. Fix: start the test-network and validate endpoints with network tools.
Error: TLS Handshake
Cause: incorrect tlsCACerts paths or hostname mismatches. Fix: point tlsCACerts.path to the CA cert and set asLocalhost appropriately for dev.

screens.title: Identity and MSP best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Identities stored in the wallet are the cryptographic actors your client uses to sign proposals. Best practice is to use clear, consistent identity names and to validate existence at startup. When creating an x509Identity, ensure the mspId exactly matches the MSP configured for that organization; mismatches lead to failures even if certificates are correct. For example, if you stored the identity under the name 'appUser', use that exact string in gateway. connect. Avoid dynamic or unpredictable identity names in production; a stable naming convention reduces human error. Also, enforce least privilege: use an application identity only with the permissions required to perform its tasks. A common misconception is that the wallet's content is only for convenience; in reality, wallet management and secure storage are a core part of your application's security posture. Closing question: what process will you use to rotate or revoke identities in your deployed systems? Identity and MSP best practices means validate identity names, match msp ids exactly, and follow least privilege principles when selecting identities for gateway connections.. fullNarratorScript:
The Fabric Gateway is the central simplification layer your client application uses to talk to a Hyperledger Fabric network. Instead of managing multiple direct connections to peers and ordering services, your app speaks to a Gateway peer using a single, well-defined A P I. This reduces complexity, lowers the chance of orchestration bugs, and makes it practical to maintain secure signing of transactions with identities stored in a wallet. In this lesson you will learn what the Gateway does, how to establish a connection from a Node. js client using a connection profile and a stored identity, and why discovery options and lifecycle management matter in both development and production. For example, enabling service discovery lets the Gateway learn which peers can endorse a transaction at runtime, so your application does not need hard-coded peer lists. A common development pitfall is using localhost certificates without the asLocalhost flag; we will show how that happens and how to avoid it. By the end, you'll be able to connect, sign, and gracefully disconnect from the Fabric network while handling common errors. How will you structure your app to reuse connections and report helpful errors to users?

By the end of these screens you will be able to explain why the Gateway is the preferred client entry point for Fabric, configure and connect a Node. js client using a connection profile and a wallet identity, and choose the correct discovery options for development versus production. You will practice handling common connection errors and learn how to manage the gateway lifecycle so your application frees resources and stays resilient. For example, you will learn how to check the wallet for an identity and how gateway. connect uses that identity to sign transactions. You will also see how service discovery reduces brittle, hard-coded peer lists and why asLocalhost is a development convenience that should be turned off for production. These outcomes matter because production applications must be secure, maintainable, and able to recover when network components change. What will you change first in your client app after this lesson?

This second objectives screen focuses on practical skills: verifying the wallet identity exists before connecting, interpreting TLS handshake errors and certificate path issues, and implementing retries for transient network failures. You will practice reading the connection profile and validating tlsCACerts paths so certificate verification can succeed. We also underscore correct MSP ID usage when creating x509Identity objects because a mismatch causes authentication failures. For development you will learn why asLocalhost=true maps hostnames to localhost for TLS verification when test certificates use localhost, and why that must be changed for production systems. Finally, you will run a sample app that logs each step—loading the profile, opening the wallet, connecting the gateway, and disconnecting—so you can see what success and failure look like in the terminal. Mastering these practices prevents common runtime issues and makes your client reliable and debuggable in real deployments.

The Gateway is the SDK component that acts as a smart proxy between client applications and a Fabric network. Define it as a single, high-level interface that handles proposal distribution, endorsement collection, and interaction with the ordering service via a designated Gateway peer. Practically, think of the Gateway as a concierge at a large building: instead of calling every room directly, you give your request to the concierge who knows where to route it and collect approvals. For example, when your application wants to submit a transaction, the Gateway arranges which endorsing peers should sign the proposal according to chaincode endorsement policies and then packages the endorsed transaction for ordering. A common misconception is that the Gateway hides all network behavior; it does not erase visibility but simplifies it—service discovery still surfaces which peers are used, and you still need correct identities and connection profiles. The core takeaway is that the Gateway reduces the amount of topology and endorsement orchestration your app must perform, letting you focus on business logic. How might this change the structure of your client code when you move from a proof-of-concept to a production app?

When a client connects to the Gateway, it establishes a connection to a specific peer or set of peers that act as a Gateway peer. That peer then performs service discovery on behalf of your application, returning information about endorsing peers, chaincode policies, and the ordering service. This dynamic discovery is what keeps your client resilient to topology changes: if a peer goes offline or a new peer joins, discovery updates let the Gateway route proposals to available endorsers without modifying the connection profile. For example, enabling discovery in the Node. js SDK instructs the Gateway to ask the connected peer which peers can satisfy the endorsement policy for a given chaincode. A common misunderstanding is believing discovery replaces the connection profile; it does not. The connection profile still provides initial endpoints and TLS certificate locations. Service discovery simply augments that runtime with up-to-date topology information. Practically, use discovery. enabled:true in production to avoid hard-coded peer lists, and ensure firewall rules allow peer-to-peer communication that discovery requires. What checks will you add to ensure discovery can reach peers in your environment?

The gateway. connect call requires a connection profile and an options object. Understanding each option is essential to make a reliable connection. The wallet option points the Gateway to a Wallets. newFileSystemWallet instance so the Gateway can retrieve the x509 credentials to sign proposals. The identity option is a string naming the stored identity; every transaction and query is signed by that identity. Discovery options are typically an object with enabled and asLocalhost flags. discovery. enabled:true turns on service discovery, which you want in production to learn topology dynamically. discovery. asLocalhost:true is a development convenience used when test networks generate TLS certs with localhost hostnames; it tells the SDK to override connection-hostnames with localhost during TLS verification. A frequent misconception is to leave asLocalhost:true in production. Doing so masks hostname mismatches and weakens certificate verification. A concrete example: gateway. connect(ccp, { wallet, identity: 'appUser', discovery: { enabled: true, asLocalhost: true } }) will work for a local test-network, but for a deployed cluster you should set asLocalhost to false and ensure your connection profile has real hostnames that match certificate SANs. What verification will you build into startup scripts to detect mismatched hostnames?

Let's walk through the typical Node. js call that opens the Gateway connection and what each line accomplishes. First, you create a new Gateway instance and prepare your connection profile and wallet. Next, gateway. connect is called with the profile and options. The wallet contains the enrolled identity that will sign proposals, so the connect call retrieves the identity and prepares the client TLS and signing material. If discovery is enabled, the gateway asks the connected peer for the endorsement layout and orderer information. Important runtime checks include verifying that the wallet contains the named identity and that the connection profile file exists and points to correct TLS certificate paths. A concrete example from the chapter shows the single-line call with options: gateway. connect(ccp, { wallet, identity: 'appUser', discovery: { enabled: true, asLocalhost: true } });. A common mistake is not checking for a missing identity before connecting; always call await wallet. get('appUser') and handle null. Closing question: when you structure your startup code, where will you add validation so connection failures are caught early and reported with clear remediation steps?

Robust applications wrap gateway connection logic in try/catch/finally so resources are always released and errors are informative. The chapter provides a full app. js pattern: declare gateway outside the try block so finally can access it, load and validate the connection profile, initialize the wallet, check the presence of the appUser identity, call gateway. connect, and then disconnect in the finally block. This pattern ensures that even if connect fails or an exception is thrown later, gateway. disconnect is attempted, preventing resource leaks. A concrete, hands-on example logs each step: loading the profile, initializing the wallet, finding the identity, attempting to connect, and disconnecting. A common misconception is that disconnect is only needed on normal shutdown; in fact, an uncaught failure that skips disconnect can leave file handles or sockets open. For long-running services, open the Gateway once at startup and reuse it rather than connect/disconnect per transaction. Reflect: where in your code will you centralize gateway lifecycle management so that retry logic and observability are simple to add? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The asLocalhost flag in discovery configuration instructs the SDK to override hostnames in the connection profile with localhost during TLS verification. This is useful when using the test-network because generated TLS certificates often have localhost hostnames. In development, setting asLocalhost to true prevents TLS handshake failures caused by hostname mismatches. However, in production this should be false since production networks use real DNS names or IPs that must match certificate SANs during verification. A concrete contrast: on a developer machine with test-network, asLocalhost:true prevents errors where the certificate lists peer0. org1. example. com but the endpoint is localhost. In production, forcing localhost would hide real hostname mismatches and could break certificate validation or security. Long-running applications should open a single Gateway connection at startup and reuse that gateway object for the application's lifetime. Opening and closing connections for every transaction is inefficient and will add latency and resource consumption.
